past_medical_history: Childhood sexual abuse (disclosed to therapist 1 year ago)

social_history.recent_stressor: Three-month anniversary of the death of a patient who died in her care during a resuscitation — she was the code team leader; subsequent hospital review process; survivor guilt

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Reports 'going somewhere else' during episodes — dissociation. Tearful when discussing work events.
neurological_exam.motor: Left arm weakness 3/5 on formal testing. POSITIVE Hoover sign — left hip extension returns to 5/5 with contralateral right leg flexion resistance. Arm falls slowly on arm drift test rather than promptly as in organic hemiparesis.
neurological_exam.sensory: Left hemisensory loss — stops exactly at the midline on face, truncal testing. Vibration intact throughout both sides.
neurological_exam.coordination: Normal right. Cannot test left arm formally due to apparent weakness.
neurological_exam.gait: Left leg dragging. Observed to walk normally when exiting elevator with colleagues.
neurological_exam.additional: As an ICU nurse, patient has witnessed and managed functional episodes in patients before. She is ambivalent about her own diagnosis. Arm falls slowly during drift test — in organic UMN lesion, arm drops promptly with pronation.

patient.chief_complaint: Left-sided weakness and episodes of dissociation/unresponsiveness — 4 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. A is a 38-year-old ICU nurse who presents with a 4-week history of left arm and leg weakness and episodes of dissociation with partial unresponsiveness. She has been the lead nurse on several overnight resuscitations and approximately 3 months ago a young patient died during a code that she led. The hospital conducted a review process that, while concluding she acted appropriately, was stressful and prolonged. She has been experiencing intrusive memories of the resuscitation, avoidance of code situations, sleep disturbance, and survivor guilt. Her current neurological symptoms began approximately 3 weeks after the anniversary of that patient's death. The episodes of unresponsiveness have occurred 4 times: each lasting 1-3 minutes, she reports feeling like she 'leaves her body,' is aware but unable to respond, with immediate recovery and full recollection of what occurred during the episode. Her colleague witnessed one episode in the staff break room: patient was sitting, eyes half-open but unresponsive to voice, no limb movements, full recovery within 2 minutes. She has migraines with aura controlled on topiramate. She is worried her topiramate is causing cognitive side effects (word-finding difficulties, which is a known side effect). She denies that her symptoms could have a psychological basis, stating 'I know what real neurological disease looks like.'

additional_observations: No posterior or parieto-occipital white matter signal abnormality
Normal cortical ribbon pattern; no cortical or subcortical diffusion abnormality
mri.impression: Normal brain MRI without and with contrast. No restricted diffusion, no T2/FLAIR signal abnormality, no abnormal enhancement, no mass effect. No white matter lesions. Normal cortical ribbon pattern. Clinical correlation recommended.

background.description: Normal symmetric 9.5 Hz posterior dominant rhythm. No focal slowing.

findings.morphology: NO EEG CHANGE during entire episode. Normal continuous background. Remarkably, patient REPORTED the content of nursing staff conversation correctly post-episode ('you said not to page the attending') — this demonstrates preserved awareness despite apparent unresponsiveness. No ictal pattern.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL EEG. One clinical dissociative episode was captured. The EEG showed continuous normal background activity throughout the episode with no ictal correlate, no electrodecrement, and no post-event slowing. No epileptiform discharges. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Normal MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine. No intramedullary signal abnormality, no cord compression, no demyelinating plaque, no leptomeningeal enhancement. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: PCL-5 (PTSD) 54 score (H), PHQ-9 15 score (H), Peritraumatic Dissociation Questionnaire 38 score (H).

EMG_NCS.test: Left upper and lower extremity NCS

FND_Physio_Response.value: Normal walking without drag by day 6

warnings: Topiramate is associated with dose-dependent cognitive side effects including word-finding difficulties (aphasia-like symptoms) and processing speed slowing. These are common at doses above 50 mg/day but can occur at lower doses in sensitive individuals.
Current dose 50 mg/day total is at the lower end — consider dose reduction to 25 mg/day if cognitive effects are causing functional impairment

Topiramate's neurological side effect profile (word-finding difficulty, processing speed slowing) is distinct from the motor and sensory symptoms being evaluated; the drug interaction query is limited to pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions
alternatives: Alternative migraine prophylaxis: amitriptyline, propranolol, valproate — note amitriptyline/SNRI may be preferred given concurrent PTSD

output.query: functional neurological disorder healthcare workers nurses occupational stress

results.title: Healthcare worker burnout and functional neurological disorder

output.summary: Published case series and surveys document FND presentations among healthcare workers in the context of occupational trauma and burnout. Survey data suggest that healthcare workers with medical knowledge frequently experience greater difficulty accepting psychological or neurobiological explanations for neurological symptoms compared to non-healthcare populations. Randomised trial evidence supports trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for PTSD-related functional neurological presentations. FND-specific physiotherapy combined with psychological treatment has demonstrated benefit in cohort studies of patients with comorbid PTSD and FND.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.
No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

advanced_imaging.impression: No abnormality identified on advanced imaging. Findings are non-contributory; clinical correlation recommended.

specialized_test.impression: Study within normal limits. No abnormality identified; non-contributory.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder — functional left hemimotor syndrome and dissociative PNES, with comorbid PTSD

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive-appearing events; ictal video-EEG showing absence of electrographic correlate during a captured habitual event is the key differentiator.
Sensorimotor symptoms in a young adult raise demyelinating disease; brain (and when indicated spine) MRI without T2/FLAIR lesions or enhancement argues against an active demyelinating process.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

FND is involuntary; preserved effort on symptom-validity testing and absence of clear secondary gain argue against feigning. The rule-in signs do not distinguish FND from malingering by themselves, but the clinical context does not support a feigning explanation.

optimal_actions.action: Elicit positive rule-in signs on bedside examination (Hoover sign for functional leg weakness, tremor entrainment / distractibility for functional tremor, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline splitting). Diagnosis of FND is made by these positive signs, not by exclusion alone.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: At least one reliable positive functional sign documented

optimal_actions.action: Order brain MRI with and without contrast to exclude a structural cause of the presenting deficit
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No structural lesion, mass, demyelination, or stroke
optimal_actions.guideline_source: FND criteria pack — exclude structural cause

optimal_actions.action: Order basic laboratory workup (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12) to exclude common reversible mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No metabolic, thyroid, or B12 abnormality that explains symptoms
optimal_actions.guideline_source: FND criteria pack — exclude reversible causes

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature on FND diagnostic signs and evidence-based treatment (CBT for PNES, specialized physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirms multidisciplinary CBT + physiotherapy is the evidence-based treatment for FND

optimal_actions.action: Obtain video-EEG monitoring with intent to capture a habitual event (prolonged inpatient video-EEG is the gold standard for distinguishing PNES from epileptic seizures)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Captured event with no ictal EEG correlate during clinically apparent seizure-like activity
optimal_actions.guideline_source: ILAE PNES Task Force minimum diagnostic standards

optimal_actions.action: Review current medications for agents that may exacerbate symptoms (e.g., benzodiazepines, dopamine-blocking antipsychotics, AEDs initiated for PNES)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identification of medication contributors that should be tapered or discontinued

optimal_actions.action: Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs; explicitly state the diagnosis is FND, the symptoms are real and involuntary, and there is an evidence-based treatment plan
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient understanding and treatment engagement — strong predictor of recovery

optimal_actions.action: Refer to specialized FND-informed physiotherapy (for functional motor symptoms) and to CBT / psychological therapy (for PNES and comorbid mood / anxiety)

useless_tools.rationale: ECG has no diagnostic role in FND; cardiac etiology is not on the differential for the presenting neurological deficit.
Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

critical_actions: Document at least one positive rule-in sign (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, distractibility, give-way pattern, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split)
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural pathology
Obtain video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG to confirm PNES
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not start or continue long-term anti-epileptic drugs for functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizures — AEDs are ineffective for PNES and expose the patient to side effects
Do not give benzodiazepines as abortive therapy for witnessed PNES events (no benefit and risk of respiratory depression)
key_reasoning_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).
Brain MRI and basic labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12) are due-diligence to exclude structural and reversible causes — they are NOT the route to the diagnosis, which is established at the bedside.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).
Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG is diagnostic for PNES (ILAE PNES Task Force 2013); routine EEG alone is insufficient.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of epilepsy in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of epilepsy does not establish the patient's events as epileptic. Video-EEG capturing the habitual event without ictal correlate is the gold standard.

red_herrings.data_point: Symptom onset coincident with a major psychosocial stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.

metadata.notes: Straightforward FND in ICU nurse with PTSD from patient death. Dissociative PNES with preserved memory during episodes is diagnostic.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Clear positive rule-in signs (Hoover sign and/or distractible tremor and/or non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) with normal MRI and supportive normal labs. Workup is hygiene-level; the diagnostic challenge is communication, not investigation.
